prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All winter she’s been growing more powerful. Radiant, says the man at the bar. Voluptuous, says the docent. Nervy, says God. All winter her soul has been juddering. It feels like drinking gold flakes! The word sleeps inside the stone. The wind tongues the underside of the lake. Inside the rifle scope of time, God teaches her Grounding Techniques through his emissary, a Certified Therapist. Beetles bore their dirty traffic into pine trees. God says, You cling to deixis like a life raft. Here, you say. Now, you say. All winter, you say, like it means something, days crossed off your compulsive calendar, wind tied to your wrist like a pet. This dumb hunger for fixity! I made your cells to shed, says God. See them everywhere, everywhere. She bites her lip till it bleeds. Who wouldn’t immanentize the eschaton, if they could, build heaven on earth in the backyard? She wouldn’t, is who. Day a slit-throated ewe. She wears a prayer around her neck in another language, no clue what it says. Who will translate the prayer? Listen: she loved a happy libertine and thought that was heaven. To ground herself she strips berries from the juniper bushes. Well, says God, Alexander the Great dyed his hair saffron. We are all made fools in this world.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A woman’s turbulent winter-long search for stability and transcendence unfolds through surreal natural imagery, divine dialogue, therapy, prayer, and memories of love. She ultimately confronts the inevitability of change and human folly, revealing that neither grounding rituals nor earthly visions of heaven can provide lasting fixity.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: All, Radiant, Voluptuous

outputs.L1:
All winter, she’s been growing more powerful. Radiant, says the man at the bar. Voluptuous, says the docent. Nervy, says God. All winter, her soul has been juddering. It feels like drinking gold flakes. The word sleeps inside the stone. The wind tongues the underside of the lake. Through the rifle scope of time, God teaches her Grounding Techniques by way of his emissary, a Certified Therapist. Beetles bore their dirty traffic into pine trees.

God says, You cling to deixis like a life raft. Here, you say. Now, you say. All winter, you say, as though it means something—days crossed off your compulsive calendar, wind tethered to your wrist like a pet. This dumb hunger for fixity! I made your cells to shed, says God. See them everywhere, everywhere.

She bites her lip until it bleeds. Who wouldn’t immanentize the eschaton if they could—build heaven on earth in the backyard? She wouldn’t, that’s who. Day, a slit-throated ewe. She wears a prayer around her neck in another language, with no clue what it says. Who will translate the prayer?

Listen: she loved a happy libertine and thought that was heaven. To ground herself, she strips berries from the juniper bushes. Well, says God, Alexander the Great dyed his hair saffron. We are all made fools in this world.
outputs.L2:
Throughout the cold season, her strength has steadily increased. The stranger drinking at the counter calls her luminous; the museum guide describes her as lush; God labels her audacious. For months, her spirit has trembled within her, a sensation like swallowing flecks of precious metal. Language lies dormant in rock. Gusts lick beneath the frozen water.

Viewed through time’s crosshairs, God sends a licensed counselor to instruct her in methods for anchoring herself. Beetles carve their grimy routes through the pines. God tells her that she grips words of place and moment as though they could keep her afloat: *here*, she insists; *now*; *the whole winter*. She treats these terms as if they possess real weight, marking each date off her obsessive calendar and tethering the wind to her arm like a domesticated creature. What a foolish craving for permanence. God reminds her that her body was designed to cast off its own cells. Look—they are scattered all around.

She chews her lip until blood appears. Given the chance, who would not try to bring the final paradise into the present and construct heaven in the yard behind the house? She is the one who would refuse. The day resembles a sheep with its throat cut. Around her neck hangs a prayer written in a language she cannot understand. Who can render its meaning for her?

Hear this: she once loved a cheerful hedonist and mistook that love for paradise. Seeking steadiness, she plucks berries from juniper shrubs. God replies that Alexander of Macedon colored his hair with saffron. In this life, every one of us is eventually made ridiculous.
outputs.L3:
Over the course of the winter, the woman becomes increasingly powerful, even as her inner life remains troubled. Her soul trembles with anxiety, uncertainty, and a persistent sense of instability. The strength she acquires does not free her from fear; instead, power and vulnerability grow alongside one another.

God speaks to her through the voice of a therapist, challenging her desperate attachment to particular places, moments, and routines. She longs for permanence, treating familiar settings and repeated actions as safeguards against disorder. Yet the therapist’s words insist that nothing can be held still. The natural world confirms this lesson: everything changes, withers, and decays. Even the woman’s own body is designed to shed and replace its cells. Change is therefore not an interruption of life but one of its fundamental conditions.

Despite this reminder, she continues to search for something tangible that will steady her. She bites her lip, gathers juniper berries, and wears a prayer whose meaning she cannot translate. These physical gestures and symbols become makeshift anchors. Their value lies less in what they signify intellectually than in the sense of presence and continuity they provide.

Her memories offer another kind of refuge. She recalls loving a carefree libertine, a figure whose freedom once seemed to open a path toward heaven. In remembering him, she also mourns a lost vision of transcendence—a time when joy, desire, and abandon appeared capable of overcoming fear. Yet this vision cannot be recovered intact. God’s final judgment is both humbling and universal: whatever power people gain and whatever certainties they pursue, the world ultimately makes fools of everyone.
outputs.L4:
Over the course of a long, unsettled winter, a woman searches for something solid enough to anchor her life. The world around her seems at once ordinary and enchanted: snow, animals, trees, darkness, and sudden changes in weather take on symbolic force, reflecting her fear, desire, loneliness, and hope. Nature does not merely surround her; it appears to speak in a surreal language, offering fleeting visions of order while continually reminding her that everything living is subject to transformation.

Her search moves between the sacred and the practical. She speaks with God, sometimes in reverence and sometimes with anger, demanding explanations for suffering and instability. She attends therapy, trying to translate spiritual confusion into the language of memory, emotion, and human need. She prays, repeats familiar rituals, and attempts to ground herself in the body and the immediate world. Yet each method provides only temporary relief. Faith cannot eliminate uncertainty, therapy cannot make the past disappear, and ritual cannot prevent the future from arriving.

Memories of love deepen the conflict. She recalls intimacy as a kind of refuge—a place where another person once seemed capable of making life coherent. Those memories are tender but unreliable, shaped by longing and loss. Love promises transcendence, yet it is also vulnerable to time, misunderstanding, and separation. What once felt permanent becomes another shifting image, beautiful precisely because it cannot be held.

As winter continues, the woman imagines versions of heaven within earthly life: a peaceful landscape, a healed relationship, a harmonious self, a world in which suffering has finally acquired meaning. Each vision briefly persuades her that stability is possible. But these private heavens dissolve. The natural world changes, relationships alter, beliefs falter, and even the self refuses to remain fixed. Her efforts to create permanence reveal the limits of human understanding and the folly of believing that life can be fully controlled.

By the end of her search, she has not discovered a final refuge or an unchanging truth. Instead, she confronts the inevitability of change. Stability, she realizes, cannot mean stopping time or escaping uncertainty. Neither prayer, therapy, memory, love, nor communion with nature can produce lasting fixity. They can offer moments of clarity, consolation, and connection, but no permanent shelter from impermanence.

Her revelation is therefore both painful and liberating. Human beings are foolish in their repeated attempts to possess what must pass, yet those attempts are also part of what makes them human. The desire for transcendence survives even when every earthly vision of heaven proves temporary. In accepting that nothing can remain unchanged, the woman begins to understand that meaning may lie not in achieving permanence, but in continuing to love, pray, remember, and endure within a world that is always becoming something else.
outputs.L5: All around her, the garden shimmered beneath the summer sun. Radiant blossoms opened toward the light, filling the air with rich perfume, while voluptuous roses spilled over the old stone walls in waves of crimson and gold. For one perfect moment, everything felt abundant, vivid, and alive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, lyrical prose poem about a woman becoming more powerful over the winter while arguing with God about time, change, faith, and the human desire for permanence.
counterfactuals.output:
All winter, she argued with God in the orchard.

The trees stood around them like black nerves, each branch remembering a fruit it could no longer hold. Snow fell upward some nights. Other nights, the moon descended into the well and drank until morning.

“You made time badly,” she told God, splitting kindling with one clean stroke.

God, who had taken the shape of a white fox, licked the bright wound of the axe. “You say that because it takes what you love.”

“I say it because it calls theft change.”

The fox vanished beneath the fence. God returned as wind, worrying the shutters, slipping cold fingers beneath the door.

At first she was small with grief. She wore three sweaters and still trembled. She kept old letters in the oven so their words would stay warm. She set two cups at the table—one for herself, one for the life that had left her—and every evening the empty cup filled slowly with darkness.

“Faith,” said God from inside the chimney, “is drinking what you cannot see.”

“Then you drink it,” she answered, and poured the darkness onto the floor.

It crawled away like ink seeking a sentence.

By January, her hair had grown long enough to snare the constellations. Orion struggled above the roof until she loosened one braid. She learned to carry fire in her bare hands. The wolves began leaving gifts at her threshold: a silver rib, a clock without numbers, the blue tongue of a bell.

“You are changing,” God said, now speaking through the frozen river.

“So are you.”

“I do not change.”

She knelt and struck the ice. A crack ran from her fist to the horizon.

“Then why do you keep changing your voice?”

For seven days there was no answer. The silence deepened, feather by feather, until the world seemed buried beneath a great white bird. She walked into the forest and found all her former selves sleeping upright among the pines: the child with blood on her knee, the bride with rain in her veil, the widow—or almost widow—the woman who had mistaken endurance for obedience. Their faces shone under the bark.

She touched each one.

They opened their eyes inside her.

By February, she no longer shivered. Winter itself came to warm its hands at her body. She ate icicles and spoke in thunder. When she stepped across the lake, the fish rose beneath her feet like a moving crown.

“You want permanence,” God said, appearing at last as an old woman seated in the snow, mending a torn hour with red thread.

“I want nothing beautiful to vanish.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It is exactly the same thing.”

The old woman smiled, and every wrinkle became a road leading somewhere the woman had been afraid to go.

“If nothing vanished,” God said, “where would you put tomorrow?”

The woman looked toward her house, its windows lit by all the dead she had loved. They waved from the glass, cheerful and impossible. Behind them, clocks bloomed on the wallpaper, each with petals instead of hands.

She wanted to run to them. She wanted to nail the moment shut.

Instead she lifted her arms.

The house rose into the air, shook snow from its roof like a great animal, and flew south.

“Cruel,” she whispered.

“Perhaps,” said God.

“Necessary?”

“Perhaps.”

“I hate your perhaps.”

“It is the hinge of faith.”

Then the woman laughed—a sound so fierce the mountains dropped their ancient names. The sun, startled, broke open under the earth. Sap began its slow ascent. In the fields, seeds turned in their sleep.

She took the red thread from God and tied it around her wrist.

“Not to keep the hour,” she said.

“No?”

“To remember I survived it.”

When spring came, it did not conquer her. It asked permission.

She stood in the orchard, taller than the thaw, with stars tangled in her hair and winter burning quietly in her palms. Buds opened wherever she looked, but she did not call them forever. She called them now.

God watched from every changing thing.

And because she had ceased demanding that the world remain, the world could no longer take itself from her.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental flash-fiction passage in which God speaks through a certified therapist, grounding techniques mingle with mystical revelation, and vivid images of winter, pine beetles, juniper berries, and lost love recur.
counterfactuals.output:
My therapist’s certificate hangs crooked behind her, gold seal glinting like a small trapped sun.

“Name five things you can see,” she says.

I see snow stitching the window shut. I see the black commas of pine beetles under the bark. I see juniper berries, blue as old bruises, trembling on the sill. I see her mouth. I see the empty chair where you refuse to stop sitting.

“Four things you can touch.”

Wool sleeve. Cold glass. My own pulse. The silence you left me.

“Three things you can hear.”

The radiator knocking. A plow passing through winter. God clearing Her throat inside the therapist.

Then her voice changes—not thunder, not trumpets, only the mild professional cadence she uses to discuss copays.

**Beloved, you keep mistaking absence for an ending.**

I look at the certificate. Licensed Clinical Social Worker. The gold seal opens one bright eye.

“My grief is not a cognitive distortion,” I say.

“No,” God says through her. “It is a forest.”

Behind her, the wall becomes pines. Beneath each scale of bark, beetles write their dark, meticulous scripture. They tunnel galleries shaped like the streets where we once walked, your mitten in mine, snow caught in your lashes. Every tree is dying beautifully, rusting from the inside.

“Two things you can smell,” she says.

Juniper crushed between fingers.

Your hair after snow.

The therapist leans forward. God leans forward inside her. The room tilts toward revelation, then remembers its training.

“Press your feet into the floor.”

I do. The floor is frozen earth. Below it: roots, beetles, bones, the blue bead of every unsent apology.

“Good,” she says. “Notice you are supported.”

**Even now,** says God.

Outside, winter repeats itself: white field, black tree, white field, black tree. The juniper berries knock softly against the glass, each one a tiny planet where we did not lose each other.

“One thing you can taste.”

I open my mouth.

Snow.

Pine blood.

The bitter blue of juniper.

Your name, still warm.

The therapist’s eyes fill with ordinary human tears. God withdraws without billing for the extra minute.

Before I leave, she straightens her certificate.

Behind it, something keeps tunneling.

Above us, the snow begins again—not forgiveness, exactly, but practice.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense contemporary prose poem featuring deixis, “immanentize the eschaton,” Alexander the Great dyeing his hair saffron, and a prayer written in an untranslated language. Make the tone nervy, sensual, theological, and darkly funny.
counterfactuals.output: Here, now—this is the kingdom, apparently: the laundromat at 2 a.m., its round windows spinning our minor apocalypses, your red dress tumbling with my tax forms, the machines accepting only quarters as if Caesar had franchised eternity. There, beneath the EXIT sign, God keeps failing to arrive, though every fluorescent tube trembles with advance publicity. You touch the salt behind my ear and say *immanentize the eschaton* like a safe word. I laugh too loudly. Somewhere Alexander the Great is dyeing his hair saffron, perfuming conquest, making himself radiant for the worm; somewhere his soldiers are checking their reflections in their shields and pretending history isn’t just panic wearing eyeliner. This body, that wound, those sirens—deixis is theology with a shaking finger. Behold: the vending machine dispenses one stale cake and calls it manna. Behold: my mouth at your throat, petitioning the warm republic of blood. I pray because desire has always been bad at paperwork: **Κύριε, ἐλέησον· φύλαξόν με ἀπὸ τοῦ σκότους τοῦ ἐντός, καὶ μὴ ἀποστρέψῃς τὸ πρόσωπόν σου ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ.** The dryers stop. For one luxurious second, silence removes its gloves. Then your phone lights up—LOW BATTERY, the angel announces—and we understand the joke: resurrection is scheduled, but the charger is over there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented literary monologue about a spiritually unsettled woman who compulsively marks time, bites her lip until it bleeds, and tries to ground herself in nature while God mocks her hunger for stability.
counterfactuals.output:
Three seventeen.

I write it on my wrist with a pen that has almost stopped believing in ink.

Three seventeen. The kettle clicks. The pipes knock once inside the wall. A crow tips its black cup of a body into the wind.

Three eighteen.

I bite the place already bitten. Salt, iron. A small red proof that I am still arranged around a pulse.

*

They tell me: touch the earth.

So I kneel in the garden and press both palms into the dirt. The dirt is cold, granular, busy with its buried mouths. A root threads between my fingers, pale as a vein. I say: Here. I am here.

God laughs in the leaves.

Not loudly. God has never needed volume.

A little shimmer. A little green applause.

You want permanence? He asks, making the grass bow and rise, bow and rise. Look how everything worships by leaving.

*

Four oh-six.

Four oh-seven.

I count the cracks in the paving stones. I count my breaths in sets of eight. I count the church bells, though the church has been empty for years and the bell is only a recording played through a rusted speaker.

Still, I count.

Still, my mouth fills.

*

At the river I take off my shoes.

Mud closes over my toes with the tenderness of an animal deciding whether to eat from my hand. Minnows turn their quick silver commas below the surface. I try to read what they are saying.

Begin again, perhaps.

Or: there is no beginning.

The current touches my ankles and does not stay. Nothing stays. God has built a whole world out of departures and then given me a hunger shaped like a house.

Cruel architect.

Invisible landlord.

I ask for one fixed thing.

He sends weather.

*

Five forty-two.

The sky bruises beautifully, which feels personal.

I bite down.

A drop of blood lands on a clover leaf, round and bright, and for a moment I am ashamed to have added myself to the evening.

Then an ant finds it.

Then the wind moves on.

*

I lie beneath the pine and name what holds me: needle, stone, root, gravity. I say each word slowly, as if fastening buttons.

Needle.

Stone.

Root.

Gravity.

Above me, the branches keep no time at all.

God shakes them and shakes them.

Somewhere in that dark green laughter I hear: Poor child. Poor clock-hearted child. You keep asking the hour as if the hour could keep you.

Six nineteen.

Six twenty.

Six—

I press my bleeding lip to the bark.

The tree does not answer.

The tree is alive.

For now, I decide, these are the same thing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a poetic, hallucinatory paragraph that blends barroom observations, museum language, psychotherapy jargon, biblical authority, bodily transformation, and startling pastoral violence. Use repetition, personification, and abrupt shifts between first, second, and third person.
counterfactuals.output: At the bar, the glasses gossip in their little amber tongues, and the jukebox keeps diagnosing me: attachment, abandonment, attachment, abandonment, while you cradle your beer like a reliquary labeled *Anonymous Thirst, mixed media, circa the Fall*. Observe the exquisite damage, says the wall text; note how the subject avoids eye contact with God. I tell my therapist the stools have begun to kneel, but she calls this transference, and he—who was not there, who is always there—opens the Book and declares, Let every wound become a door. So my ribs unlatch. So my ribs unlatch. Inside me a white gallery blooms, climate-controlled and full of saints with moths for faces; inside you, a shepherd counts backward from ten. Suddenly the pasture enters the room wearing blood to the elbows: lambs burst like psalms beneath the red machinery of dawn, the hills chew their cud and refuse to testify, and one astonished cow lifts its head as if subpoenaed by thunder. I am no longer a man but an exhibit of hooves and blue smoke; you are no longer forgiven but beautifully framed; she takes notes while the moon, drunk and maternal, presses its cold thumb to his forehead and says, This is my body, this is my body, this is my body—please do not touch the art.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
